title: CERN distributed information and Web software reuse
summary: A distributed information-management proposal and later reuse permissions reveal technical and institutional complements; they do not independently establish global diffusion causes.

stages.invention: 1989 proposal builds on existing hypertext ideas and author’s Enquire experience; no exclusive first-invention claim.
stages.feasibility: 1993 release names operational client/server/library components; detailed reliability benchmarks not inspected.
stages.deployment: CERN early implementation and software release, bounded by documentary evidence.
stages.diffusion: Permission for external reuse documented; no population diffusion curve acquired.
stages.non-adoption/niche: Proposal describes existing hierarchical and keyword-based systems as practical alternatives with limitations.
stages.displacement/reversal: No measured disappearance of prior systems.

mechanisms: Linking existing information lowers migration demands: design rationale, uptake effect unmeasured.
Cross-system compatibility and remote access support the specified organisational task.
Reuse permissions can lower legal entry costs; comparative importance underdetermined.
counterevidence: Existing systems were useful; later graphical interfaces or network expansion could explain wider uptake. Original proposal is not a success evaluation.

episode.technology_configuration: 1989 distributed hypertext design at CERN; separate 1993/1994 client/server/library licensing subepisode.
episode.task: Find and maintain information across changing research teams and heterogeneous computers; permit others to reuse implementation.
episode.population: CERN collaborators and prospective code implementers; worldwide adopter denominator unavailable.
contemporary_alternatives: Commercial or academic hypertext systems mentioned by proposer
episode.adoption_measure: Qualitative design and release documents; no comparable user counts or retention window.
episode.observation_limits: Institutional participant sources; proposed benefits are not measured realised adoption.

actors.chooser: CERN management could authorise work; implementers could choose software reuse. Individual adoption decisions not observed.
actors.payer: CERN and participating organisations supplied staff/computing resources; spending and payer incidence not quantified.
actors.operator_maintainer: Software developers and information contributors; distributed maintenance proposed, actual time burden unmeasured.
actors.affected_nonchooser: New researchers and colleagues whose information became findable; affected nonusers not surveyed.
actors.ability_to_refuse: A proposal and permissive reuse do not show mandatory adoption; ability of individual staff to avoid the system is unknown.

labour.tasks: Documentation retrieval, linking and updating; predecessor information transfer through people and newsletters. No net employment estimate.
labour.entry_barriers: Computing access and implementation knowledge; credential/occupation barriers not measured.
labour.bargaining_ownership: CERN controlled initial code-release terms; subsequent ownership and bargaining distribution outside scope.
labour.transition: 1989 proposal to early-1990s release chronology; no individual occupational transition evidence.
labour.distribution: The proposer expected reduced information loss, but distribution of realised time savings not measured.
labour.evidence_limit: Cannot infer displacement of librarians, administrators or developers, or net jobs from a design proposal.

title: US household computers and internet: diffusion with coexistence
summary: CPS documents rising household access; ACS joint access demonstrates that computers, handhelds and subscriptions frequently coexisted in 2015.

stages.invention: Outside episode; devices and networks pre-existed surveys.
stages.feasibility: Assumed operational availability in survey categories, not independently benchmarked.
stages.diffusion: CPS computer series 1984–2015 and internet series 1997–2015.
stages.scaling: Population reach grows; supply-side scale economies not identified.
stages.non-adoption/niche: A substantial remainder lacks each measured form of access.
stages.displacement/reversal: No wholesale replacement supported by 62% with all three categories in 2015.

mechanisms: Affordability and demographic differences as unseparated candidates
counterevidence: Co-ownership may represent different household members or idle devices; it does not itself prove beneficial task division.

episode.technology_configuration: Personal computers and home internet in CPS history; 2015 ACS desktop/laptop, handheld and broadband categories.
episode.task: Household access to computing and online services; actual task mix not measured by the headline indicators.
episode.population: US households; CPS and ACS are separately specified samples and questions.
contemporary_alternatives: Public/workplace/school access, not fully measured here
Desktop/laptop and handheld devices as coexisting options
episode.adoption_measure: CPS household computer percentages 8/51/79 in 1984/2000/2015; household internet 18/73 in 1997/2015. ACS joint access 62% in 2015, not minutes of use.
episode.observation_limits: No harmonised CPS/ACS level-splice; handheld and broadband definitions broader than smartphone/fixed broadband.

actors.chooser: Household-level access reported; individual chooser or employer influence is not identified.
actors.payer: Household and potentially employer resources; survey does not allocate payments.
actors.operator_maintainer: Household users, vendors and network providers; unpaid household technical support not measured.
actors.affected_nonchooser: Household members who did not purchase devices; excluded people required to use online services not separately observed.
actors.ability_to_refuse: Non-adoption exists, but survey does not distinguish refusal, inability to pay, disability or lack of need for every household.

labour.tasks: Potential access to information, government, banking and education; no job-task time series measured here.
labour.entry_barriers: Income/access differences observed in report; skills, hiring credentials and discrimination not causally evaluated.
labour.bargaining_ownership: Ownership of devices/subscriptions measured; ownership of platforms and bargaining power not evaluated.
labour.transition: Long household adoption series, not tracked worker careers.
labour.distribution: Demographic/geographic access differences are reported; no distribution of wages or job gains established.
labour.evidence_limit: Cannot convert household computer growth into employment creation, deskilling or productivity distribution.

title: Smartphone preference, constrained dependence and task difficulty
summary: UK preference, US dependence and later UK task-perception evidence make portable access plausible while leaving its causal ranking unresolved.

stages.feasibility: Phones, PCs and tablets already operational options; suitability depends on task.
stages.diffusion: US adult smartphone ownership 2011 to late 2014; UK 2015 importance snapshot.
stages.non-adoption/niche: Service interruptions and alternate-device preferences remain.

mechanisms: Availability away from desks as a plausible mechanism
counterevidence: Phones remain useful despite reported document difficulty; older UK internet users prefer other interfaces. Price hierarchy between laptops and phones is unestablished.

episode.technology_configuration: UK 2015 internet-device preference/household tablets; US 2011–2014 smartphones with or without other access; UK 2023 phone forms/documents perception.
episode.task: Mobile communication/internet access versus sustained document/form tasks; task differences explicit.
episode.population: UK 2015 internet users 16+ for importance, all households for tablet access; US adults 18+ for ownership/dependence; UK 2023 smartphone users 16+ for M 6A.
episode.interval: 2011/November 2014 US ownership; October 2014 panel circumstances; UK early 2015; UK Sep–Nov 2023.
contemporary_alternatives: Feature/basic phones for voice/SMS, not equivalent web/app capacity
Public or borrowed access, availability not uniformly observed
episode.adoption_measure: 33% vs 30% most-important smartphone/laptop among UK internet users 2015; 54% UK household tablet access; 64% US adult smartphone ownership late 2014 and 7% conjunctive dependence; 48% of dependent users ever suspended service financially; 68% of UK smartphone users 2023 perceive forms/documents harder.
episode.observation_limits: Different places, years and denominators are contrasts, not a pooled trajectory. Perceptions and past hardship are not objective performance or current disconnection.

actors.chooser: Individual users select devices and services within household/institutional constraints; direct chooser-payer mapping unknown.
actors.payer: Users/households and sometimes subsidised contracts; actual subsidy incidence not estimated.
actors.operator_maintainer: Users, household helpers, mobile providers and app vendors; maintenance burdens not quantified.
actors.affected_nonchooser: Other household users, correspondents required to coordinate, and people needing online forms; impacts not fully sampled.
actors.ability_to_refuse: Pew documents few alternate routes and financial interruption; this is constrained access, not evidence of freely preferred sole dependence.

labour.tasks: Pew documents job information/application use; phone interfaces support some work-related tasks but complicate forms/documents for many respondents.
labour.entry_barriers: Connectivity cost and input difficulty observed; occupational credentials and accessibility adaptations not measured.
labour.bargaining_ownership: Provider/platform control and switching costs are candidates; no bargaining-power estimate.
labour.transition: No panel of occupational transitions or time-to-retraining; device ownership series is not career evidence.
labour.distribution: Lower-income users’ dependence/financial fragility observed; no identified earnings effect.
labour.evidence_limit: Cannot infer that smartphones replace knowledge workers, equalise employment opportunity or make laptops obsolete.

title: India: mobile data expansion and unequal educational access
summary: Falling nominal revenue per GB accompanies greater service spending; household phone availability still fails to imply child access for study.

stages.feasibility: Mobile internet and smartphone learning were available but require complements not captured by subscriptions.
stages.deployment: Telecom subscription/revenue returns and household smartphone availability.
stages.diffusion: ASER restricted 2018–2021 availability comparison; rural/urban subscription density 2024.
stages.scaling: Large fall in average revenue/GB, without a causal supply explanation.
stages.non-adoption/niche: Children in phone-owning homes can lack study access; rural subscription density lower.
stages.displacement/reversal: No claim that physical schooling or basic phones were displaced.

mechanisms: Total affordability differs from per-GB prices
counterevidence: Lower unit revenue coexists with higher per-subscriber monthly revenue; phone survey excludes important non-exposure.

episode.technology_configuration: National wireless data service and subscription accounts; separate rural household smartphone access for education during pandemic disruption.
episode.task: Access internet services; children obtain study materials or participate remotely.
episode.population: Telecom subscriptions/data subscribers, not unique people; ASER enrolled rural children 5–16 in a phone-reachable sampling frame.
episode.interval: Calendar 2014 vs FY 2023–24 accounts; March 2024 density; 2018–2021 ASER comparison.
contemporary_alternatives: Printed study materials and in-person teaching when available
Computer/tablet, availability not established for all sampled children
episode.adoption_measure: Official nominal revenue per GB and per-data-subscriber/month; subscriptions per 100 inhabitants. ASER smartphone-at-home and conditional study-access shares, with no-phone households excluded from 2018 comparator.
episode.observation_limits: Do not infer unique use from subscriptions; survey mode/reachability differs; children’s access is not measured learning gain.

actors.chooser: Household adults decide acquisition/allocation; telecom providers decide offers; schools shape delivery. Individual decisions not directly reconstructed.
actors.payer: Households, service providers and educational institutions; payment/incidence data unavailable.
actors.operator_maintainer: Network operators; household device managers; teachers and caregivers supporting access. Unpaid burden not quantified in selected tables.
actors.affected_nonchooser: Children who neither purchase nor control phones; households excluded from telephone sampling.
actors.ability_to_refuse: Children cannot necessarily control use of household phones; school closure constrains in-person alternatives, but individual compulsion is not measured.

labour.tasks: Teachers’ delivery and caregivers’ support potentially reorganised; study-access allocation documented, not hours of unpaid work.
labour.entry_barriers: Device/control, connectivity, language and literacy require separate measures; no labour-market entry estimates.
labour.bargaining_ownership: Household ownership and provider service terms can constrain pupils; intra-household bargaining not identified.
labour.transition: 2018–2021 availability contrast, not a longitudinal occupational transition.
labour.distribution: ASER reports unequal access by grade and parental education; neither income effect nor causal learning distribution established.
labour.evidence_limit: Do not translate telecom scale or household smartphone availability into school achievement, employment or equal opportunity.

title: Kenyan mobile money: simple phones, agent networks and welfare estimates
summary: M-PESA’s operational complements explain how ordinary phones carry transfers; welfare estimates depend on rollout assumptions, while 2024 adoption uses a distinct adult denominator.

stages.invention: SMS money transfer built on prior practices; no Kenyan global-first claim.
stages.feasibility: Deposit, account transfer and cash redemption architecture documented.
stages.deployment: M-PESA launched 2007; agents perform local conversion.
stages.diffusion: Early user-household surveys and 2024 current mobile-money use; incompatible denominators not spliced.
stages.scaling: Agent-network expansion observed; quantified contribution conditional.
stages.non-adoption/niche: Phone/ID barriers and withdrawal delays; existing banks/cash remain alternatives.
stages.displacement/reversal: No complete displacement of banks, cash or other payment channels established.

mechanisms: Savings/risk-sharing/occupation channels examined with unresolved confounding
counterevidence: Cash shortage/outages impede use; adoption can coexist with other financial services; poverty estimates conditional and not universal fintech evidence.

episode.technology_configuration: 2007–2010 SMS M-PESA transfer/cash-agent configuration; 2008–2014 household panel welfare study; separate 2024 all-provider current-use survey.
episode.task: Send/redeem money, store value and manage financial needs; welfare outcomes include consumption and occupation.
episode.population: Early Kenyan user households in authors’ panel; 2014 estimation sample 1608 households outside Nairobi/far-north omissions; 2024 access/use among adults 18+.
episode.interval: Launch 2007; survey 2008/2009; early agent changes 2008–2010 and outcomes 2014; later snapshot 2024.
contemporary_alternatives: Other mobile-money providers, not separately estimated here
episode.adoption_measure: Early household ever-use and reported withdrawal delays; welfare model estimates, not adoption counts; 2024 current mobile-money use 82.3% adults 18+, no fixed activity window.
episode.observation_limits: M-PESA provider, all-provider mobile money, household and individual measures distinct. Panel attrition and assumed rollout exogeneity; 2024 cross-sectional usage does not replicate earlier poverty effect.

actors.chooser: Users choose transfers/accounts; Safaricom and agents choose rollout/operation; regulators shape eligibility; choice constrained by practical alternatives.
actors.payer: Users pay transfer/redemption charges; agents commit cash/e-float; institutional/provider investments. No complete incidence estimate.
actors.operator_maintainer: Agent proprietors/staff, carrier infrastructure workers and banking institutions. Informal family assistance not quantified.
actors.affected_nonchooser: Remittance recipients, dependants and excluded people lacking phones or documents; not all choose system design.
actors.ability_to_refuse: Official ID and phone constraints documented; network participation can be useful without being costless to refuse. Coercion not established.

labour.tasks: Agent cash/e-float management; remittance administration; Suri/Jack examine shifts from farming into business/sales.
labour.entry_barriers: Agent liquidity/assets and registration; users’ phones/IDs. Training, fees and gender barriers not completely measured.
labour.bargaining_ownership: Provider controls system; agents operate conversion; ownership of resulting household businesses and bargaining outcomes not fully measured.
labour.transition: Panel 2008–2014 examines occupational endpoints and authors estimate shifts, but individual transition durations and job quality not observed here.
labour.distribution: Estimated welfare gains stronger for female-headed households; causal interpretation conditional, not a universal gender benefit.
labour.evidence_limit: No net employment count, wages of agents, work quality, market-power losses or full social welfare accounting; overlapping panel evidence not replication.

title: VR gaming and prolonged computer work: three different outcome measures
summary: UK participation, German work experience and global segment finances are kept separate; none supplies a global retained-user measure.

stages.feasibility: Commercial Quest 2 used for matched virtual-desktop experiment.
stages.deployment: UK reported gaming and tested office configuration, not all VR uses.
stages.diffusion: Single 2023 UK cross-section; no valid growth estimate from summary typo.
stages.scaling: Meta 2023 segment resources/revenue, not user scaling.
stages.non-adoption/niche: VR gaming minority compared with other devices in UK 2023; experimental withdrawals in prolonged work.
stages.displacement/reversal: No evidence of broad replacement of conventional computers; no claim of permanent failure.

mechanisms: Social coordination, price and surroundings awareness remain unranked candidates
counterevidence: Younger adult VR participation higher; small long-work study does not test optimised spatial tasks; segment losses do not imply zero utility.

episode.technology_configuration: UK 2023 VR gaming-headset question; separate Quest 2/Chrome Remote Desktop/K830 week-long work setup; separate Meta FY 2023 Reality Labs accounts.
episode.task: Gaming in UK; prolonged ordinary desktop work in experiment; corporate investment/revenue accounting.
episode.population: UK adults 16+ n 3643; 16 German-university worker completers plus 2 withdrawals; Meta consolidated segment, no user denominator.
episode.interval: UK 27 Sep–12 Nov 2023; study reported Jun 2022, exact fieldwork dates not established; Meta FY ended 31 Dec 2023.
contemporary_alternatives: Physical matched display and keyboard for experiment
episode.adoption_measure: Gaming participation 4% VR vs matched device questions; no weekly/monthly threshold. Experimental subjective ratings and withdrawals; segment revenue/loss, not shipments or active users.
episode.observation_limits: No pooling across these populations/measures. Quota survey, small occupational experiment and broad commercial segment; no global installed-base/retention estimate.

actors.chooser: Individual gamers; voluntary study participants; Meta management allocates resources. These are different chooser sets.
actors.payer: Household/device purchasers unknown; study equipment provided under research design; company funds investment. Per-headset subsidy unmeasured.
actors.operator_maintainer: Users/developers/device vendors; researchers controlled test apparatus. Maintenance cost not measured.
actors.affected_nonchooser: Household members/bystanders and workers expected to use immersive interfaces are not adequately sampled.
actors.ability_to_refuse: Two participants exercised withdrawal; general consumer ability to refuse workplace VR unknown. No inference of coercion from lab results.

labour.tasks: Prolonged knowledge-work interface tested; developer/content/research work implied by company operations but employment counts not derived.
labour.entry_barriers: Hardware/access, skills and fit constraints; occupational entry pathways and credentials unknown.
labour.bargaining_ownership: Employer/vendor ownership and platform terms could matter; experiment does not identify bargaining power.
labour.transition: One week per environment, no retraining/career transition follow-up; corporate finances not worker trajectories.
labour.distribution: Individual discomfort and withdrawals observed; no distribution of wages/jobs or representative disability outcomes.
labour.evidence_limit: No inference that VR replaces offices/workers or improves/damages all productivity; subjective ratings are not output.

title: Microsoft phone hardware: sales coexist with strategic retrenchment
summary: An already deployed phone business had large unit sales while expected business value was written down; platform coordination remains a plausible, unisolated explanation.

stages.feasibility: Operational Lumia and non-Lumia products sold.
stages.deployment: 36.8 million Lumia and 126.8 million non-Lumia sales FY 2015.
stages.diffusion: Sales are a flow; installed base and active use not measured here.
stages.scaling: Full-year revenue includes acquired business, not comparable organic growth.
stages.non-adoption/niche: Narrower strategic focus announced; market-specific non-adoption unmeasured.
stages.displacement/reversal: 2015 impairment/retrenchment, without an inferred terminal platform date.

mechanisms: Acquisition valuation and execution as strong rivals
Total business economics differ from device feasibility
counterevidence: Large sales demonstrate users; an impairment is not a user-preference experiment or proof of specific ecosystem causality.

episode.technology_configuration: Post-acquisition Microsoft Phone Hardware portfolio including Lumia and other phones; company platform strategy.
episode.task: Sell communication/computing devices sustainably and build a common application ecosystem.
episode.population: Company worldwide sales and accounts; consumer population denominator unavailable.
episode.interval: FY 2015 with partial post-acquisition FY 2014 comparator; acquisition 25 Apr 2014.
contemporary_alternatives: Android/iOS phones as broad platform alternatives named in company business context
Existing PC/tablet services; not identical communication substitutes
episode.adoption_measure: FY 2015 reported unit sales plus $7.5 billion impairment and management retrenchment statement; not active users or retention.
episode.observation_limits: Partial FY 2014 comparator; no consistent global smartphone market denominator, app catalogue comparison or carrier-incentive data.

actors.chooser: Microsoft executives and developers decide investment; distributors and buyers choose stocking/use; their decisions not separately observed.
actors.payer: Corporate capital and purchasers; financing/subsidy allocations unknown.
actors.operator_maintainer: Microsoft and partner manufacturing/software/channel workers; product maintenance conditions not inspected.
actors.affected_nonchooser: Employees facing restructuring and existing users dependent on ecosystem continuity.
actors.ability_to_refuse: Company portfolio changes are not selected by affected employees/users; individual bargaining/refusal evidence absent.

labour.tasks: Engineering, manufacturing, distribution and support reorganised; report records restructuring expenses including severance but no causal net-employment effect.
labour.entry_barriers: Skills, assets, distribution access and developer audience; individual entry barriers not directly researched.
labour.bargaining_ownership: Company controls portfolio and acquisition capital; worker bargaining outcomes not described.
labour.transition: Accounting/strategy episode FY 2014–2015; no longitudinal worker destination/retraining evidence.
labour.distribution: Severance/restructuring costs reported; distribution of gains/losses across workers or countries unknown.
labour.evidence_limit: Cannot infer an occupational decline or net social loss solely from corporate impairments.
